description: Find a member by exact Member ID, fill in a new sub-account form with a given account type and initial deposit, and reach the Review New Sub-Account page. Deliberately stops there and takes no action -- it never clicks 'Confirm Creation', so no account record is actually created. riskClass: safe.

parameters.name: memberId
parameters.description: Exact Member ID to open the sub-account for (e.g. "1001"). This capability does not disambiguate multiple last-name matches.

parameters.name: deposit
parameters.description: Initial deposit for the new sub-account. Must be a positive amount.

parameters.name: accountType
parameters.description: Type of sub-account to open. Must be exactly one of the target app's actual account types -- values outside this set fail before any browser action runs.

parameters.name: slow
parameters.description: When true, appends the app's real ?slow=true testing hook to the initial login navigation, adding a genuine 2-4s server delay. Exercises the recoverable wait/retry path deterministically.

parameters.name: username
parameters.description: Back-office operator username. The mock app accepts any value, but a real target would require a real credential here.

outputs.name: reviewedAccountType
outputs.description: The account type shown back on the Review New Sub-Account page -- confirms the review step reflects the requested accountType parameter.

outputs.name: reviewedDeposit
outputs.description: The initial deposit amount echoed back on the Review New Sub-Account page -- confirms the review step captured the entered amount correctly, before any decision to actually create the account.

steps.description: Go to the top-level login page.

recoveryHints.name: retry_with_longer_wait
recoveryHints.detector: navigation did not complete within the short 1500ms probe window
recoveryHints.note: the app's ?slow=true hook adds a genuine, bounded 2-4s server delay; a 6000ms retry timeout comfortably covers the worst case, so this always resolves deterministically rather than flaking.

steps.description: Type the operator username into the login form's first field.

locator.robustnessRationale: login.ejs has no <label for>, id, or name that identifies this field semantically (the input's own name attribute is the opaque 'u'). The only stable signal is the table layout itself: a <td> containing the literal text 'Username:' immediately followed by a sibling <td> holding the input. There's no second, equally valid strategy here because there's genuinely nothing else on the page to anchor to (role+name resolves to an unnamed textbox shared with the password field, since neither has an accessible name) -- the positional xpath is the only reliable signal, which is itself the point of this fixture.

steps.description: Type the operator password into the login form's second field.

locator.robustnessRationale: Same reasoning as fill_username: no label/id/name to anchor to, so the field is identified by the adjacent 'Password:' table cell. A role-based locator (role=textbox) would match this AND the username field, since <input type=password> has no distinguishing accessible name either -- the structural xpath is the only strategy that resolves uniquely.

This is a real <input type=submit value="Log In"> -- unlike the text fields, submit inputs DO get a real accessible name from their value attribute, so role+name is genuinely reliable here and is preferred over css. The css fallback (there's exactly one submit input on this page) only matters if a future app revision changes the button's visible label.

steps.description: Type the member ID into the search box inside the dashboard's main content iframe.

frame.robustnessRationale: dashboard.ejs's main content iframe deliberately has no name or id -- BUILD-SPEC.md requires it be identifiable only by position: 'the only iframe directly under the second <table><tr><td>'. Both strategies encode exactly that structural rule; xpath is listed first because it reads closer to the spec's own wording (second table, then the iframe descendant) and is less likely to silently match an unintended element if a future revision adds another table before the nav table, whereas the css nth-of-type fallback is kept for engines/tooling that resolve css faster than xpath.

locator.robustnessRationale: search.ejs explicitly avoids <label for> by design (BUILD-SPEC.md: 'no labels via <label for> -- use visible adjacent text instead'), so there is no label-based strategy available at all. The input's name attribute ('q') is intentionally non-semantic. The only strategy that survives is the same table-adjacency pattern used for the login fields.

frame.robustnessRationale: Same main-content-iframe rationale as fill_search_query -- repeated per step because each step independently re-resolves its frame chain (the iframe is re-fetched fresh, not cached, since its own internal document changes across the flow).

locator.robustnessRationale: Real <input type=submit value="Search">, so role+name is reliable (accessible name comes from the value attribute, same reasoning as click_login_submit). css input[type=submit] is a valid fallback on this specific page because the search form is the only form present before a search has been run.

steps.description: Click the result row whose first cell equals the searched member ID -- this is a row-relative button-in-a-form, not a plain <a href>.

frame.robustnessRationale: Same main-content-iframe rationale as the earlier steps.

locator.robustnessRationale: search.ejs deliberately renders each member ID as a <button type=submit> inside a tiny per-row <form>, not an <a href>, specifically so the target member id isn't visible in a plain href (BUILD-SPEC.md). BUILD-SPEC.md's own suggested locator strategy is 'the button in the row whose first cell equals {memberId}' -- this xpath is exactly that: find the <tr> whose first <td> equals the templated member id, then its descendant <button>. normalize-space(.) (the td's full string-value) is used rather than normalize-space(text()) because the id text is inside the nested <button>, not a direct text child of the <td>. This is the only viable strategy on this page; role+name would match the button's own visible text (the id), but role alone can't disambiguate rows without the same row-relative predicate, so xpath is used directly rather than pretending a simpler strategy is equally robust.

steps.description: Inside the detail page, click the 'New Sub-Account' button, which lives in a second iframe nested inside the main content iframe.

frame.robustnessRationale: Same main-content-iframe rationale as the earlier steps -- the detail page itself renders inside this iframe, same as extract_savings_balance's checkpoint in the sibling savings-lookup capability.

locator.robustnessRationale: subaccounts.ejs renders a real <button type="submit">New Sub-Account</button> -- a genuine accessible name from its own text content, so role+name is reliable and unique (this button only renders at all when the member's status isn't 'Closed'; see the account_closed business outcome below for what happens when it's absent).

steps.description: Select the requested account type in the New Sub-Account form's dropdown.

frame.robustnessRationale: Same main-content-iframe rationale as the earlier steps.

Same nested-Sub-Accounts-iframe rationale as click_new_subaccount_button -- clicking that button replaced this same iframe's document with subaccount-new.ejs via a same-frame form submission, so the frame chain to reach it is unchanged.

locator.robustnessRationale: subaccount-new.ejs's <select name="type"> has no label/id to anchor to (name='type' is non-semantic and not exposed as an accessible name), so it's identified by the adjacent 'Account Type:' table cell -- the same table-adjacency pattern used throughout this app's forms. The <option>s' own value attributes ('Savings'/'Checking'/'CD') are exactly the accountType parameter's allowedValues, so {{accountType}} always names a real option.

steps.description: Type the initial deposit amount into the New Sub-Account form.

frame.robustnessRationale: Same main-content-iframe rationale as the earlier steps.

Same nested-Sub-Accounts-iframe rationale as click_new_subaccount_button -- clicking that button replaced this same iframe's document with subaccount-new.ejs via a same-frame form submission, so the frame chain to reach it is unchanged.

locator.robustnessRationale: subaccount-new.ejs has no label/id/name to anchor to (name='deposit' is non-semantic and not exposed as an accessible name), so the field is identified by the adjacent 'Initial Deposit:' table cell -- the same table-adjacency pattern used throughout this app's forms.

steps.description: Check the 'I confirm I want to open this sub-account' checkbox -- required before the form will submit.

frame.robustnessRationale: Same main-content-iframe rationale as the earlier steps.
Same nested-Sub-Accounts-iframe rationale as fill_deposit.

locator.robustnessRationale: The checkbox has no id/name-based label -- its only association is the adjacent 'Confirm:' cell (the confirmation sentence after it, 'I confirm I want to open this sub-account', is plain sibling text inside the same <td>, not a <label for>). Same table-adjacency pattern as fill_deposit; 'click' toggles the checkbox on since it starts unchecked.

steps.description: Submit the New Sub-Account form to advance to the review step.

Same nested-Sub-Accounts-iframe rationale as fill_deposit.

locator.robustnessRationale: Real <input type=submit value="Review">, so role+name is reliable (accessible name from the value attribute). css input[type=submit] is a valid fallback since it's the only submit control on this form.

steps.description: Read the Account Type echoed back on the Review New Sub-Account page. This is the last step -- no 'Confirm Creation' click follows, so no account record is ever created.

frame.robustnessRationale: Same main-content-iframe rationale as the earlier steps.
Same nested-Sub-Accounts-iframe rationale as fill_deposit -- subaccount-review.ejs is this same iframe's document, replaced in place by click_review_submit's form submission.

locator.robustnessRationale: subaccount-review.ejs renders fields as LabelValue rows with no id/class, identical convention to detail.ejs -- the value is found by the same row-relative pattern used for extract_savings_balance in the sibling savings-lookup capability.

steps.description: Read the Initial Deposit echoed back on the Review New Sub-Account page.

frame.robustnessRationale: Same main-content-iframe rationale as the earlier steps.
Same nested-Sub-Accounts-iframe rationale as fill_deposit.

locator.robustnessRationale: Same row-relative convention as extract_reviewed_account_type -- 'Initial Deposit' is the row label used on the review page. This should equal the deposit parameter, confirming the review step reflects what was actually entered.

checkpoint.description: The nested Sub-Accounts iframe shows the 'Review New Sub-Account' page -- the flow stops here, one step before the irreversible create action.

frame.robustnessRationale: Same main-content-iframe rationale as the step-level frame chains above.
Same nested-Sub-Accounts-iframe rationale as the step-level frame chains above.

locator.robustnessRationale: The checkpoint re-checks the review page's own heading -- text-content match first (cheapest, what an operator would actually read), with a structural xpath pinned to the <h3> as a fallback in case similar wording appears elsewhere on a future revision of this page.

businessOutcomes.name: member_not_found
businessOutcomes.description: The searched member ID has no matching record -- a real, expected business outcome, not a crash (BUILD-SPEC.md's canonical 'business outcome, not failure' case).

frame.robustnessRationale: Same main-content-iframe rationale as the step-level frame chains above -- the not-found message renders inside the same iframe as the search results table would have.

detector.robustnessRationale: search.ejs renders exactly this literal string in a single-cell row when results.length === 0, whether triggered by a genuine non-match or by ?fail=not_found. Text match is preferred as the primary strategy since it's exactly what a human operator would read; the xpath fallback pins it to the specific table cell in case the surrounding copy ever changes wording elsewhere on the page.

outputs.name: message
outputs.description: The literal not-found message shown to the operator.
